And this young man, Mr. Smith, he asked, called me up and asked me to come up and talk to the high school kids. Well, I did, but it's too much of a chore for me to go up those steps and that. I said, I just won't be able to do that. But I said, what I'd like to do is have the kids come over here and feel free to ask me anything they want to about the book. And I can have 10 or 15 at a time if they want to. They'll sit on the floor or anything. And I've done that for two winters now, and this winter too. And then I've done quite a lot for the museum. The museum people have taken several recordings. And the kids, of course, now when I come up there to the high school, they'll come here too. They like to know more about the Moscow history. That is the difference with one. The one of them just couldn't get over me telling them about that island and the churches. Why did they build 33 churches on that island? Did you say the Romans did that? Yes. In 11, about 1100 they came up there. Not to conquer, but to Christianize the island. And then I said, well, you must remember, they couldn't go to church at all if there had only been one church on that island. The only way they could get there was either walk or else ride behind the oxen. And most likely they had oxen then, I said, even in 1100. But now, of course, they've got automobiles. And when I went there in 53, they didn't even have automobiles. They had one or two automobiles, and a cousin of mine had gotten back from America, and she hired one of those cars to take us around and show us the island. And they didn't know how to drive. Well, let's back up a little bit now. Your mother was Mary Lynd, and when was she born? Do you know that? No, let's see. I better go. Is that in the book? Yeah, let's see. No, it's not, because see, I got a separate book for that. I got a little appendage for the book that I sent to all the family. Oh, I see. And it's got all the birth dates and that in it. But then 1873, I think June 9, 1873. June 9, 1873. And where was she born? She was born in Sweden, in Germany. But she was only a very small child when she came with her parents. And her parents came to America, so she came with them as a small child. And they came to Minnesota, and they lived there from, I imagine they came about 1860s or 70s. Maybe about 1875 that they came to Minnesota. Then they decided to come out to Idaho. And she said this, I told that in the book. She told the Sunday school teacher, she went to the Presbyterian Church because there wasn't any Scandinavian church. And she went to Sunday school, but I guess the parents didn't go. They just read their catechism, and they were Lutheran, of course. But, you see, the Church of England, of Sweden, was Catholic, all of them were, until the Reformation. Even England, all of them were. And then it became Lutheran during the Reformation, after Lutheran, during the Renaissance. I shouldn't know all my history real well, because I've read a lot of it. Yes, you've read up a lot about this for your trip. Yeah, well, you know. What did you... Would that be right? Why don't I just look it up? Well, we'll look it up later. Why don't you just sit here now? We'll go back and find out. Well, I'm sure that's right about her birthday. And my father was 12 years older, so he would subtract that from 13, or from 73, it'd be 60. Yes. 60. 1860. Yeah. Where was he born? He was born in November. His birthday was 59. 1859. 1859. All right. And where was he born? Well, he was born on this island. Oh, this island. It was originally, you know how they did in Italy and everywhere, they were separate, nearly every city was a separate state. They had their own rulers and everything. And this island didn't become a part of the Swedish crown. It was written in the German, Russian. And it became part of the Swedish crown when... in chemistry at the University of Minnesota. He had three choices, Seattle, Northwestern, or Minnesota. And he took Minnesota because it was good for his chemistry research work. He'd already done a lot of research work in Gdansk. And when he was going to get here and finish all his work, and one instructor wanted him to work with him for, I think, two months or weeks, maybe. I don't know how many weeks. And they were going to have the announcement of engagement on Iowa Grove. I don't know where it was, there, but he met her there, not in the school. They were batching. A whole bunch of graduate students had apartments and were batching. And they were going to have a party, and some of the instructors were going to be there, too. And this girl had announced her engagement that afternoon, or evening. He was to go downtown on an errand to get some things for this party. And a class medic who was attending, getting his doctorate in Seattle, he came by there on his way to Washington and stopped to see him. And the girl said, well, you get Bill, or whatever his name was, to go with you, because I'm kind of tired, and then we'll get things lined up here for the party. And she waited there and sat there and waited for him. And there they got a call that both of them had been killed in an auto accident. Both those boys. And oh, I feel like my chest is killing me every time I think of it. It was so terrible. It seemed like I couldn't do it. And Whitey and I were here, and he went into his room and I went into the classroom. And we were about ready to go to dance party. And he came out and he said, Elsie, be prepared for the worst. And I said, when in the world could it happen? He said, that was the call. He had a phone in his room. That was the call from Elvera and Boyce, and Bill has been killed in an auto accident. And we just both came in and just couldn't. Both of us cried. It was just awful. Well, we won't take no more time to ask. That was interesting, though. What were your brothers' names? Yeah, my brother's name. The oldest one was? Yeah, the oldest one. I think I better write him down. Oh, I can... Can you? Yes. Well, it's Fredolf. We always called him Fritz. Fredolf, I think it's German. Fre-F-R-D-B-L-E. Some cousin or somebody named him. D-O-L-P-H. D-O-L... P-H. But you called him Fritz. Yeah. And then Carl Phillip. Carl Phillip. He's the second one. He's the one who lives in California. Doing real well. And... And then Oscar. Oscar was named after his dad, August. Oscar... Carl Kim Whitey. Yeah. Nobody in town really knows him by any other name. Businessmen don't. And... Fred Eugene. That's the cousins. I got tired of naming them when there were too many. There were seven. They let him name some of them with more modern names. And Theodore. He was named after an uncle. Theodore. We're not in the second name. No, that first name will be in... Theodore. Well, it's Theodore. And we called him T.N. lots of times. And... Then David Reynolds. He graduated from Idaho with... And he's been in the Air Force. And he's been with Air West since he graduated. He was in the Government Air Force. Department of Commerce Bureau of Aeronautics. Through the war. Second World War. And then he... After that, while he worked in... Well, it was... You're not getting that. You're not... I just want to... Is that the recorder? Yeah. Well, let me cut it down. Well, here. I'll cut some of that off. And then, let's see. David Reynolds. With the Aeronautics Man. And then Enoch. E-N-O-T-H. We call him Nick. He's a jeweler in Louisiana. Married a French girl. French nurse. Okay, and you had seven brothers then. And the two sisters. Two. Two brothers gone. Alright, now this is information about you yourself. Your personal information. What education... What education did you have? Well, I got a lot for those times. I want to start with the first three weeks. You read about that in the book. And then I started in the Moscow City School. Finished high school. 1909. By that time, I already had 12 credits in college. Because I went to both places. Oh, simultaneous. And I had 12 credits in college when I started. At the university in the fall. And you started at the university then in that fall. In 1909. Fall of 1909. And then I graduated in 1912. I was supposed to graduate in 1915. 1915 would have been my class if I hadn't... taken that extra work. Then I took one year of graduate work in Home Ec. Of course, I'd taken Home Ec. all the way through. So I got... Some of my Home Ec. friends... You got more education in Home Ec. than we have. But you got your first degree, wasn't it in sociology? In biology. Botany was my major. I used to... I substituted it. Only when the professor left, I took over his lab class. So you were kind of teaching assistants. Yeah. We had to really... I did. It was both German and biology for educational credit. Because I got my certificate to teach. So those were teaching assistants which helped. Which was necessary for a teacher certificate of that kind. I don't think they do that now. I don't know. All right. Then besides teaching, which is one of your skills, you could do cooking, then. You know why I don't like that? Why? Well, because it made me so mad at the hotel. There wasn't any of my friends or any of my queens that said anything about it. But once in a while, I'd hear different people talk or introduce me or something. And they'd say, well, she's the cook. That's a lot of difference between being in charge. Yeah, cook and being manager. You were the manager then. I'll tell you what my... for our AAUW, I belonged to. They gave me... I was supposed to be director of food at the Moscow Hotel. And I was. I was director and manager of the food department at the AAUW. And that was a stiff job, I want you to know. Got up at five o'clock every morning out there, seven days a week. Once in a while, I had to go to the hospital to rest my legs. I had to plan, do all the planning. I didn't plan all the meals. I didn't plan the meat courses for the daily menu. But I planned the rest of the menu. And the chef planned the meat courses. And I did all the ordering. I had to help. Discharge them. But I didn't do that because I didn't believe in that. I didn't fire anybody. I had to fire anybody. I said, girls, you'll have to help me out. I said, just tell that girl that if she doesn't do better work than that, I'll just one night keep you here. That's all they had to say. But the next day she's gone. I never fired anybody. I got along with my maidens. I got along with my maidens.
